title: What is Astrology?
description: A plain introduction to astrology as a symbolic language of planets, signs and houses, and how to use it for reflection.
content:
## A language of symbols

Astrology is a way of reading meaning into the positions of the Sun, the Moon and the planets as they appear from Earth. Astrologers treat the sky as a set of symbols, a little like the vocabulary of a language. Each planet stands for a kind of energy or need, each sign describes a style, and each area of the chart points to a part of life.

The most useful way to think about astrology is as a tool for reflection and planning. It gives you words and images for thinking about your temperament, your relationships and the rhythm of your year. It does not decide what happens to you, and it does not replace your own judgment.

## Where astrology comes from

People have watched the sky for as long as there have been people. Astrology as we know it grew out of Babylonian sky-watching around 2,500 years ago, was shaped by Greek thinkers in Hellenistic Egypt, and then passed through Persian, Arabic and medieval European traditions. Separate traditions also developed in India (often called Jyotish, or Vedic astrology) and in China.

For most of that history, astrology and astronomy were the same field. Over the past few centuries they split apart. Astronomy became the physical science of stars and planets. Astrology stayed a symbolic and interpretive practice.

## The building blocks

Almost everything in Western astrology comes from four ingredients. Each has its own lesson in this section, so here is just a first look.

• Planets: the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and Pluto. Astrologers call all ten "planets" for convenience, even though the Sun is a star and the Moon is a moon. Each one is associated with a part of your inner life, such as feelings (the Moon) or drive (Mars).
• Signs: the zodiac is a band of sky that the Sun, Moon and planets travel through. Astrologers divide it into twelve equal sections of 30 degrees each, called signs, from Aries to Pisces. A sign describes how a planet tends to express itself.
• Houses: the chart is also split into twelve houses, each linked to an area of life such as home, work or friendship. Houses depend on the exact time and place of birth.
• Aspects: these are the angles between planets. They show which parts of the chart tend to work together and which tend to pull against each other.

Here is a short worked example. Suppose you were born on 5 May. On that date the Sun sits in the sign of Taurus, so you are said to have your "Sun in Taurus." The Sun is associated with your core identity and sense of purpose. Taurus is associated with steadiness, comfort and patience. Many astrologers read a Taurus Sun as someone who tends to build slowly and value what lasts. That single sentence is astrology in miniature: a planet, a sign, and an interpretation.

## Which zodiac?

Traditions differ on where the signs begin. Most Western astrologers, and this app, use the tropical zodiac, which ties the start of Aries to the March equinox, the point in spring (for the Northern Hemisphere) when day and night are about equal. The signs follow the seasons. Vedic astrology and some Western astrologers use the sidereal zodiac, which ties the signs to the background stars instead. Because of a slow wobble in Earth's axis, the two now differ by about 24 degrees, so the same person can have a different Sun sign in each system. Neither is a mistake; they measure from different starting points.

## Is astrology a science?

No. Astrology is a symbolic tradition, not a science. Controlled studies have not found reliable evidence that planetary positions predict personality or events, and there is no known physical way for distant planets to shape a person's character. It is honest to say this plainly.

That does not make astrology useless. Many people find value in it the way they find value in poetry, mythology or a journal prompt. A chart can offer a fresh angle on a question, a vocabulary for talking about differences between people, or a reason to pause and check in with yourself. The value comes from the reflection it prompts, not from any claim to certainty.

A few habits help you use it well:

• Treat readings as questions, not verdicts. "Does this fit me?" is more useful than "This is who I am."
• Notice what resonates and what does not. Both tell you something.
• Keep real decisions grounded in real information. Astrology can help you think about timing or feelings, but it is not medical, legal or financial advice.
• Be kind in how you use it with others. A sign is never a good reason to judge someone.

Then go to the Charts tab and open Birth Chart to see your Big Three (your Sun, Moon and Rising signs) and your Planet Positions. As you work through the next lessons, come back to that screen and match each new idea to something in your own chart.

title: The Birth Chart
description: What a birth chart is, what you need to make one, and how to read its planets, signs, houses and aspects step by step.
content:
## What a birth chart is

A birth chart, also called a natal chart, is a map of the sky at the moment and place you were born. It shows where the Sun, the Moon and the planets were, as seen from your birthplace, and it arranges them on a circle. Astrologers treat this map as a symbolic portrait: a set of themes you can reflect on, not a script your life must follow.

Every chart is built from the same parts. What makes yours personal is the particular combination of positions at your birth. Two people born on the same day in different cities, or a few hours apart, will share many planet positions but can have quite different charts overall.

## What you need to make one

To calculate a birth chart you need three pieces of information:

• Your date of birth. This places the Sun and most planets in their signs.
• Your time of birth, as exactly as you can find it. This sets the Rising sign and the houses, and it fixes the Moon's exact position, since the Moon moves quickly.
• Your place of birth. The town or city gives the latitude, longitude and time zone, which the calculation needs.

If you do not know your birth time, AstroNumeric assumes 12:00 noon. The planets in their signs will still be mostly right, but the Rising sign and houses become estimates, and the app flags this so you know which parts to hold loosely. The lesson "Why Your Birth Time Matters" explains this in detail.

## Reading the wheel

A chart is drawn as a wheel. Think of it as the sky wrapped around you, with Earth at the center.

• The horizontal line across the middle is your horizon. Its left end is the Ascendant, or Rising sign: the sign that was rising over the eastern horizon when you were born. Its right end, the Descendant, is the point setting in the west.
• The top of the chart is the Midheaven, often labeled MC, the highest point the Sun reaches in the sky that day. The bottom is the IC, the point directly below you.
• The twelve slices of the wheel are the houses. They are numbered counterclockwise, starting from the Ascendant.
• Around the outside run the twelve signs, from Aries to Pisces.
• Small symbols, called glyphs, mark where each planet sits.
• Lines drawn across the middle connect planets that form aspects, meaning particular angles to each other.

The wheel can look busy at first. You do not need to take it in all at once. The app also lists the same information as plain text, which is easier for beginners.

## Four layers: planets, signs, houses, aspects

A helpful way to read any part of a chart is to ask four questions in order.

• What? The planet tells you what kind of energy or need is involved. Venus is associated with love, pleasure and values.
• How? The sign tells you the style. Venus in Gemini tends to express affection through talk, curiosity and variety.
• Where? The house tells you the area of life. Venus in the 3rd house points to siblings, neighbors, writing and everyday conversations.
• With what else? The aspects tell you which other planets are involved. If Venus makes a square (a 90 degree angle) to Saturn, many astrologers read tension between wanting closeness and feeling cautious.

Put together, you get a sentence you can reflect on: "My sense of what I value and enjoy (Venus) tends to come out through words and ideas (Gemini), especially in daily conversations and local life (3rd house), with a streak of caution I have to work with (square Saturn)."

## A worked example

Take someone born on 15 June 1990. The Sun sign is Gemini, because Gemini runs from about May 21 to June 20. So the Sun, associated with core identity and purpose, sits in a sign associated with curiosity and communication.

Now suppose this person was born at 7:00 in the morning. Around sunrise, the Sun is near the Ascendant, so their Sun would likely fall in the 12th or 1st house. If they were born around noon instead, the Sun would sit near the Midheaven, around the 9th or 10th house, an area linked with career and public life. Same date, same Sun sign, but a different emphasis. This is why the time matters so much.

When you start reading your own chart, begin with the Big Three: your Sun sign (your core self), your Moon sign (your emotional needs), and your Rising sign (how you tend to meet the world). Then look at where the Sun and Moon sit by house. That alone gives you plenty to reflect on before you move on to every planet and aspect.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Go to the Charts tab and open Birth Chart. At the top are your Big Three: Sun, Moon and Rising. Below that, Planet Positions lists each planet with its sign and house, Key Aspects shows the most important angles between planets, and Houses shows which sign begins each house. Pick one planet and practice the four questions: what, how, where, and with what else.

title: Planets & Their Meanings
description: A guide to all ten planets astrologers use, from the Sun to Pluto: what each means and how long it stays in a sign.
content:
## What planets mean in astrology

In astrology, a planet stands for a part of you: a need, a drive or a way of functioning. If a birth chart is a story, the planets are the characters. The sign a planet is in describes its style, and the house describes where in life it tends to show up.

Astrologers use ten bodies and call them all "planets" for convenience. Strictly, the Sun is a star and the Moon is Earth's moon; together they are called the luminaries, meaning the lights. Each planet also has a home sign, called the sign it rules, where its qualities are thought to come through most naturally.

Speed matters too. A fast planet changes sign often, so it varies a lot from person to person. A slow planet stays in one sign for years, so everyone born in that stretch shares it. That is why astrologers group the planets into three sets.

## The personal and social planets

The first five, the personal planets, move quickly and are read as the most individual parts of a chart.

The Sun is associated with your core identity, vitality and sense of purpose. It is the "who am I" of the chart. The Sun spends about a month in each sign and takes a year to go all the way around, which is why your Sun sign depends on your birthday. It rules Leo. Example: someone with the Sun in Capricorn is often described as purposeful and patient, drawn to building something that lasts.

The Moon is associated with emotions, comfort, instinct and what you need to feel safe. It moves fastest of all, spending only about two and a half days in each sign and circling the zodiac in about 27 days. It rules Cancer. Example: a Moon in Aries often suggests feelings that flare quickly and pass quickly.

Mercury is associated with thinking, speaking, learning and everyday errands. It never strays far from the Sun in the sky, so it is usually in the same sign as your Sun or one next to it. It rules Gemini and Virgo. Example: Mercury in Gemini tends to think fast and enjoy conversation; Mercury in Virgo tends to think carefully and notice detail.

Venus is associated with love, pleasure, beauty, taste and what you value, including money. It also stays close to the Sun. It rules Taurus and Libra. Example: Venus in Taurus is often linked with enjoying physical comfort, good food and loyalty.

Mars is associated with drive, courage, desire, anger and how you go after what you want. It takes about two years to circle the zodiac and usually spends six to seven weeks in a sign, though longer when it appears to slow down. It rules Aries. Example: Mars in Capricorn is often read as ambition that is disciplined and strategic.

Jupiter and Saturn, called the social planets, move more slowly and are often read as connecting your personal life to the wider world.

Jupiter is associated with growth, optimism, learning, generosity and meaning. It takes about 12 years to circle the zodiac, so it spends about a year in each sign. It rules Sagittarius. Example: Jupiter in Cancer is traditionally considered a strong placement, often read as generosity expressed through care and family.

Saturn is associated with structure, responsibility, limits, time and maturity. It can feel like a strict teacher, but many astrologers see it as the planet of what you build through effort. It takes about 29 and a half years to circle the zodiac, spending about two and a half years in each sign. It rules Capricorn. Example: Saturn in Libra is often read as taking relationships and fairness seriously.

## The outer planets

Uranus, Neptune and Pluto were discovered with telescopes between 1781 and 1930, so ancient astrologers did not use them. They move so slowly that astrologers often read their signs as themes shared by a whole generation. Their house position and aspects in your chart are more personal.

Uranus is associated with change, independence, originality and sudden breaks from routine. It takes about 84 years to circle the zodiac, around seven years per sign. In modern astrology it rules Aquarius; traditionally, Saturn did.

Neptune is associated with imagination, dreams, compassion, spirituality, and also with confusion and blurred boundaries. It takes about 165 years to circle the zodiac, around 14 years per sign. In modern astrology it rules Pisces; traditionally, Jupiter did.

Pluto is associated with power, depth, transformation and what is hidden. Its orbit is uneven, so it spends anywhere from about 12 to 31 years in a sign, and roughly 248 years to go all the way around. In modern astrology it rules Scorpio; traditionally, Mars did. Astronomers reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006, but astrologers still use it.

## Retrograde and other points

Sometimes a planet appears to move backward through the zodiac for a while. This is called retrograde. The planet is not really reversing; it is an optical effect of Earth and the other planet moving at different speeds, like a car you pass on the highway seeming to slip backward. Every planet except the Sun and Moon goes retrograde at times. Many astrologers read a retrograde planet as energy that turns inward or asks for review. Mercury retrograde, which happens about three times a year, is the best known.

Your chart may also list a few extra points. The North Node is a calculated point where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path; many astrologers read it as a direction of growth. Chiron is a small body between Saturn and Uranus, often read as a sensitive spot that can become a source of wisdom. Some asteroids appear as well. They are optional extras; the ten planets are the core.

## A quick summary

• Sun: identity and purpose. Rules Leo.
• Moon: feelings and needs. Rules Cancer.
• Mercury: mind and communication. Rules Gemini and Virgo.
• Venus: love, pleasure and values. Rules Taurus and Libra.
• Mars: drive and action. Rules Aries.
• Jupiter: growth and meaning. Rules Sagittarius.
• Saturn: structure and responsibility. Rules Capricorn.
• Uranus: change and independence. Rules Aquarius.
• Neptune: imagination and compassion. Rules Pisces.
• Pluto: depth and transformation. Rules Scorpio.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Go to the Charts tab, open Birth Chart, and scroll to Planet Positions. Each planet is listed with its sign and house, and retrograde planets are marked. Start with your personal planets, the Sun through Mars, and read each one as a sentence: this part of me (planet) tends to act in this style (sign). The same list also shows the North Node, Chiron and some asteroids.

title: Houses in Astrology
description: What the twelve houses are, how they are calculated, and the area of life each one is associated with.
content:
## What the houses are

If the planets are the characters in a chart and the signs are their styles, the houses are the settings: the areas of life where things tend to happen. The birth chart wheel is divided into twelve slices, and each slice, called a house, is associated with a theme such as money, home, work or friendship.

Houses come from the Earth's daily spin, not from the planets' paths. As the Earth turns, the whole zodiac appears to rise in the east and set in the west once a day. The houses freeze that turning at the moment you were born. Signs change every month or so; houses change every couple of hours. That is why houses depend on your exact birth time and place, while your Sun sign depends only on your birthday.

## How the houses are drawn

The line where a house begins is called its cusp. The most important cusp is the Ascendant, the sign rising on the eastern horizon at your birth, which begins the 1st house. From there the houses are numbered counterclockwise around the wheel. The Midheaven, the highest point of the sky, usually marks the start of the 10th house.

Astrologers have several ways to divide the chart, called house systems, and traditions differ. Placidus, a system from the 1600s, is the most widely used in modern Western astrology and is what AstroNumeric uses by default. In Placidus, houses can be different sizes. Other popular systems include Whole Sign, where each sign is one whole house and which is common in ancient and Vedic practice, and Equal House, where each house is exactly 30 degrees. A planet near a cusp can land in a different house depending on the system, so if another app disagrees by one house, this is often the reason.

If you do not know your birth time, AstroNumeric assumes 12:00 noon. The houses are then estimates, and the app flags this.

## The twelve houses

The first six houses are often read as more personal, and the last six as more about other people and the wider world. Each house also has a natural partner: the sign in the same position in the zodiac, starting with Aries for the 1st.

• 1st house: the self, your body, appearance and first impressions. It begins at the Ascendant. Natural sign: Aries.
• 2nd house: money, possessions, resources and self-worth, meaning what you value and what you feel you are worth. Natural sign: Taurus.
• 3rd house: communication, learning, siblings, neighbors, short trips and daily routines of thought. Natural sign: Gemini.
• 4th house: home, family, roots and private life. It begins at the IC, the bottom of the chart. Natural sign: Cancer.
• 5th house: creativity, play, romance, fun, self-expression and children. Natural sign: Leo.
• 6th house: daily work, habits, health routines, service and the tasks that keep life running. Natural sign: Virgo.
• 7th house: close partnerships, both romantic and business, and one-to-one relationships, including open rivals. It begins at the Descendant. Natural sign: Libra.
• 8th house: shared resources, intimacy, trust, debts, inheritances and deep change. Natural sign: Scorpio.
• 9th house: beliefs, higher education, travel, philosophy and the search for meaning. Natural sign: Sagittarius.
• 10th house: career, reputation, public role and long-term goals. It usually begins at the Midheaven. Natural sign: Capricorn.
• 11th house: friends, groups, communities, networks and hopes for the future. Natural sign: Aquarius.
• 12th house: rest, solitude, the unconscious, endings, and what happens behind the scenes. Natural sign: Pisces.

The four houses that begin at the Ascendant, IC, Descendant and Midheaven (the 1st, 4th, 7th and 10th) are called angular houses. Many astrologers treat planets there as especially visible in a person's life.

## Reading a planet in a house

To read a house placement, combine the planet, the sign and the house into one sentence. Suppose your chart shows Mars in Virgo in the 10th house. Mars is associated with drive, Virgo with precision and usefulness, and the 10th house with career. Many astrologers would read this as ambition that tends to show up through careful, practical work in a public role.

Here is a second example. The Moon in the 4th house joins the planet of emotional needs with the house of home and family. It is often read as a strong need for a secure, comfortable home base.

## Empty houses and house rulers

Ten planets spread across twelve houses means at least two houses are always empty, and usually more. An empty house does not mean that area of life is missing or doomed. It usually means it is not a major focus.

To read an empty house, look at the sign on its cusp and that sign's ruling planet. If your 7th house is empty and begins in Taurus, look at Venus, the ruler of Taurus. Where Venus sits in your chart adds to the story of your partnerships. Astrologers call this the house ruler.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Go to the Charts tab, open Birth Chart, and look at Houses. It lists which sign begins each of your twelve houses. Then check Planet Positions, which shows the house each planet falls in. Find which houses hold the most planets, and read the matching themes above. If you entered no birth time, remember that the app has flagged the houses as estimates.

title: Aspects: How Planets Interact
description: How the angles between planets, called aspects, show which parts of a chart work together and which pull against each other.
content:
## What an aspect is

An aspect is an angle between two planets in a chart. Picture the chart as a circle of 360 degrees. Each planet sits at a point on that circle. Measure the distance between two planets around the circle, and certain distances count as aspects.

Astrologers read aspects as conversations between planets. The planets say what parts of you are involved, and the aspect says how they tend to get along. Some combinations tend to flow easily, some create friction, and some merge into one. Aspects are often what make two people with the same Sun sign feel so different.

## Measuring angles and orbs

Each sign covers 30 degrees of the circle, so a position is written as a number of degrees within a sign, such as 10 degrees Aries. To find the angle between two planets, count the signs between them and adjust for the degrees.

Here is a worked example. The Sun is at 10 degrees Aries and the Moon is at 12 degrees Leo. From Aries to Leo is four signs (Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, then Leo), and four signs is 4 x 30 = 120 degrees. The Moon is 2 degrees further along, so the exact distance is 122 degrees. That is very close to 120 degrees, which is a trine.

Planets rarely sit at an exact angle, so astrologers allow a margin called the orb. In the example above, the trine is 2 degrees from exact, so it has a 2 degree orb.

The tighter the orb, the stronger the aspect is usually thought to be. How wide an orb to allow is a matter of tradition and taste. Many astrologers allow around 6 to 10 degrees for the major aspects, more for aspects involving the Sun or Moon, and only 1 to 3 degrees for minor aspects. AstroNumeric shows the orb for each aspect, so you can see how close each one is.

## The major aspects

These five angles are the core set used by nearly every Western astrologer.

• Conjunction (0 degrees): two planets sit together, usually in the same sign. Their energies blend and act as one, which can intensify both. Example: Venus conjunct Mars often joins affection and desire.
• Sextile (60 degrees): two signs apart. Often read as an easy opportunity, a helpful link that tends to work best when you take some action.
• Square (90 degrees): three signs apart. Often read as tension or friction between two needs. Squares can be uncomfortable, and many astrologers see them as a source of drive and growth.
• Trine (120 degrees): four signs apart, usually in the same element (fire, earth, air or water). Often read as natural ease and talent, sometimes so easy that it is taken for granted.
• Opposition (180 degrees): six signs apart, on opposite sides of the chart. Often read as a pull between two sides that asks for balance. Oppositions frequently play out in relationships with other people.

## Minor aspects

The app also shows some minor aspects, which are usually read as subtler influences.

• Semi-sextile (30 degrees): one sign apart. The two planets are in neighboring signs that have little in common, so this is often read as a mild adjustment.
• Semi-square (45 degrees): half a square. Often read as low-level irritation or restlessness that nudges you to act.

Minor aspects add detail. Beginners can safely focus on the major five first.

## Easy and hard, reconsidered

Traditional books sometimes call trines and sextiles "good" and squares and oppositions "bad." Most modern astrologers find that too simple. An easy aspect can mean comfort without much growth, and a hard aspect can mean effort that builds real skill. It is more useful to ask what each aspect asks of you than to score it.

The planets involved matter as much as the angle. A square between the Moon and Saturn is often read as feelings meeting a sense of duty or restraint. A square between Mercury and Jupiter is often read as big ideas that can outrun the details. Same angle, different conversation.

When reading an aspect, try this sentence: "My [first planet's theme] and my [second planet's theme] tend to [blend / cooperate / create friction / seek balance]." For Sun trine Moon: "My sense of purpose and my emotional needs tend to cooperate." That gives you something concrete to test against your own experience.

Aspects are also used when comparing charts. In compatibility work, called synastry, astrologers look at the angles between one person's planets and another's.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Go to the Charts tab, open Birth Chart, and look at Key Aspects. Each entry names two planets, the aspect between them and its orb. Start with the tightest orbs and any aspects involving your Sun or Moon, and try the sentence above for each one. To see aspects between two people, open Compatibility or Synastry under Advanced Charts.

title: Transits and Timing
description: How astrologers compare the planets' current positions with your birth chart to reflect on the timing of phases in your life.
content:
## What a transit is

Your birth chart is a snapshot. The sky, of course, keeps moving. A transit is the current position of a planet compared with your birth chart. When a planet in today's sky forms an aspect (one of the meaningful angles covered in the previous lesson) to a planet in your birth chart, or moves through one of your houses, astrologers say it is transiting that point.

Astrologers use transits to think about timing: which themes are likely to feel active now, and which phases of life are beginning or ending. Transits do not make events happen. They are a way of framing a period so you can reflect on it and plan with some intention.

To avoid confusion, astrologers use two words. Natal means a position in your birth chart. Transiting means a position in the sky right now. So "transiting Jupiter conjunct natal Venus" means Jupiter is currently at the same point where Venus was when you were born.

## Fast and slow transits

Speed shapes how a transit is read.

• The Moon moves about 13 degrees a day and changes sign every two and a half days. Its transits are brief and are usually read as passing moods.
• The Sun, Mercury, Venus and Mars move quickly enough that their transits last from a day or two to a few weeks. They are often read as short-term focus or energy.
• Jupiter and Saturn take a year or more to move through a sign. Their transits last months and are often read as chapters of growth or consolidation.
• Uranus, Neptune and Pluto move so slowly that their transits can stretch across one to three years. Many astrologers read them as long, deep shifts.

A good rule for beginners: pay more attention to slow transits for big-picture themes, and use fast transits for day-to-day planning.

## A worked example: the Saturn return

Saturn takes about 29 and a half years to go all the way around the zodiac. So, somewhere around age 29, transiting Saturn comes back to the exact place it occupied when you were born. This is called the Saturn return.

Saturn is associated with structure, responsibility and maturity. Many astrologers read the Saturn return as a period of taking stock: asking which commitments, jobs, relationships or habits still fit, and which need to change. A second Saturn return comes around age 58 or 59. Jupiter has a similar cycle, returning to its birth position roughly every 12 years, around ages 12, 24, 36 and so on, often read as a time of fresh growth.

These ages are shared by almost everyone, which is a good reminder that transits describe common human seasons, not a fixed personal fate.

## Retrogrades and moon phases

A planet is retrograde when it appears, from Earth, to move backward through the zodiac for a while. It is an optical effect, not a real reversal. Many astrologers treat a retrograde period as a time to review, revise and finish rather than start. Mercury retrograde, about three times a year for roughly three weeks, is often linked with rechecking plans, messages and travel details. A sensible reading is simply "double-check," not "nothing can go right."

The Moon's phases are another simple timing tool. The new moon, when the Moon is dark, is often used for setting intentions. The full moon, about two weeks later, is often read as a time of culmination, visibility or release. Eclipses are new or full moons that fall near the Moon's nodes (the two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path), and many astrologers read them as turning points.

## Other timing methods

Transits are not the only method. Traditions differ, and many astrologers combine several.

• Secondary progressions move the birth chart forward symbolically, one day after birth for each year of life. Your chart at 30 days after birth is read as your progressed chart at age 30. They are often read as slow inner development.
• Solar returns look at the chart for the moment the Sun returns to its birth position each year, near your birthday, and read it as a theme for the year ahead.

Numerology offers its own timing cycles, such as the Personal Year, which some people like to compare with transits.

Timing in astrology works best as a planning aid. If a slow Saturn transit is underway, you might choose to focus on steady, long-term work. If Mercury is retrograde, you might leave extra time to proofread a contract. Keep the reading as a prompt for reflection and let real-world information make the decision.

Temporal Matrix lets you set your calendar events against the sky. For progressions and a yearly overview, open the Charts tab and choose Advanced Charts, then Progressions or Year Ahead.

title: Why Your Birth Time Matters
description: Why the exact time you were born shapes your Rising sign, houses and Moon, and what to do if you do not know it.
content:
## Why a few hours make a difference

Your birthday alone tells an astrologer which sign the Sun was in and, roughly, where the other planets were. But a birth chart is also tied to the Earth's daily spin, and that part depends on the clock.

As the Earth turns once every 24 hours, all twelve signs of the zodiac appear to rise over the eastern horizon, one after another. The sign rising at the moment you were born is your Ascendant, or Rising sign. On average, a new sign rises about every two hours. So two people born on the same day in the same town, but four hours apart, will usually have different Rising signs.

## What the birth time controls

Several important parts of your chart depend on the time.

• The Rising sign (Ascendant): the sign on the eastern horizon at birth. Many astrologers read it as the way you tend to meet the world and the first impression you give. It is one of your Big Three, alongside your Sun and Moon.
• The Midheaven: the highest point of the sky at birth, linked with career and public life. It also moves about a sign every two hours.
• The houses: the twelve areas of life are measured from the Ascendant and Midheaven, so every house shifts with the time. The planets' signs stay the same, but the houses they fall in can change.
• The Moon's exact position: the Moon moves about 13 degrees a day, roughly half a degree an hour. On most days that only changes its degree. But the Moon changes sign every two and a half days, so if it moved signs on the day you were born, the time decides your Moon sign.

The Sun, Mercury, Venus and Mars move much more slowly, so the birth time rarely changes their signs. The exception is a birth on a day when one of them changed sign.

## A worked example

Take someone born on 15 June 1990. Their Sun is in Gemini whatever the time, because the Sun spends about a month in each sign.

Now imagine two versions of that person. One was born at 6:00 in the morning and the other at 6:00 in the evening. At sunrise the Sun is near the eastern horizon, so the morning birth tends to have the Sun near the Ascendant, often in the 12th or 1st house, and a Rising sign at or near Gemini. At sunset the Sun is near the western horizon, so the evening birth tends to have the Sun near the Descendant, around the 6th or 7th house, and a Rising sign roughly opposite Gemini, near Sagittarius. Same birthday, same Sun sign, but a very different emphasis: the first chart puts the self in the foreground, the second puts partnerships and daily work there.

How quickly the Rising sign changes also depends on the sign and on how far from the equator you were born. Some signs rise in well under an hour at some latitudes and others take closer to three. That is why even 15 minutes can matter for someone born close to the change from one sign to the next.

## If you do not know your birth time

Many people do not know their exact birth time, and a chart is still useful without it. Here are some places to look:

• Your birth certificate. Some countries and regions record the time and some do not; a long-form certificate is more likely to include it.
• Hospital or medical records from your birth.
• Family members, baby books, or letters and announcements from the time.

If you only have a rough time, such as "early morning," use your best estimate and treat the Rising sign and houses as provisional. Enter the local clock time and the place of birth; the place is what lets the chart work out the time zone.

When no birth time is given, AstroNumeric assumes 12:00 noon. Noon is a common choice because it keeps the Moon within about half a day's movement, roughly 6 or 7 degrees, of its true position either way. Your planets' signs are still mostly reliable, but the Rising sign and the houses become estimates, and the app flags this in your chart so you know which parts to hold loosely.

Some astrologers offer rectification, which means estimating a birth time by working backward from major life events. It can be interesting, but it is a matter of interpretation, and different astrologers can arrive at different times.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Go to the Charts tab and open Birth Chart. Look at your Big Three, especially your Rising sign, and at the Houses section. If you entered no birth time, the app shows a note that these are estimates based on noon. If you later find your birth time, update your profile and compare the new Rising sign and houses with the old ones.

title: The 12 Signs
description: A beginner's tour of all twelve zodiac signs, with each one's dates, element, modality, ruling planet and key traits.
content:
## What a zodiac sign is

The zodiac is a band of sky that the Sun, the Moon and the planets appear to travel along, as seen from Earth. Astrologers divide this band into twelve equal slices of 30 degrees each, and each slice is a sign. When someone says "I'm a Leo," they mean the Sun was passing through the Leo slice on the day they were born. That is their Sun sign.

AstroNumeric uses the tropical zodiac, the system most Western astrologers use. It ties the signs to the seasons: Aries always begins at the March equinox, the day in March when daylight and darkness are roughly equal. Vedic (Indian) astrology uses a different system, the sidereal zodiac, which lines the signs up with the star constellations and currently places most planets about one sign earlier. These are two traditions, not a right and a wrong answer. Every date in this lesson is tropical.

The dates are approximate. The Sun enters each sign at a slightly different moment each year, so the boundaries shift by about a day. If you were born on the first or last day of a sign (often called being "on the cusp"), your birth chart, a map of where the Sun, Moon and planets were at the moment you were born, gives the exact answer.

## Four things to know about each sign

Each sign is described by four pieces of information. Later lessons go deeper into each.

• Dates: when the Sun passes through the sign each year.
• Element: fire, earth, air or water. The element describes a sign's basic temperament. Fire is associated with energy and enthusiasm, earth with practicality, air with ideas and communication, and water with feelings.
• Modality: cardinal, fixed or mutable. The modality describes how a sign tends to act. Cardinal signs start things, fixed signs keep them going, and mutable signs adapt them.
• Ruler: the planet linked to the sign, also called its ruling planet. The ruler lends the sign some of its character. Three signs have both a modern and a traditional ruler, and both are given below.

The traits that follow are tendencies, not a personality test. Your full chart contains all twelve signs somewhere, and most people recognize parts of themselves in several.

## Aries to Virgo

Aries (Mar 21–Apr 19). Fire, cardinal, ruled by Mars. As the first sign, Aries is associated with beginnings: courage, directness, a quick start and sometimes a quick temper. It tends to act first and reflect later. Its growth area is patience and finishing what it starts.

Taurus (Apr 20–May 20). Earth, fixed, ruled by Venus. Taurus is linked with steadiness, comfort, the physical senses and loyalty. It tends to build slowly and hold on to what it values, whether that is a friendship, a routine or a good meal. The other side of that steadiness can be stubbornness.

Gemini (May 21–Jun 20). Air, mutable, ruled by Mercury. Gemini is associated with curiosity, conversation and quick thinking. It enjoys variety, learning a little about many things, and connecting people with ideas. It can scatter its attention or grow restless.

Cancer (Jun 21–Jul 22). Water, cardinal, ruled by the Moon. Cancer is linked with home, family, memory and care. It tends to protect the people it loves and to feel things deeply, sometimes behind a guarded outer shell. Moodiness and holding on to old hurts are its common challenges.

Leo (Jul 23–Aug 22). Fire, fixed, ruled by the Sun. Leo is associated with warmth, creativity, generosity and self-expression. It often enjoys being seen, and it likes making others feel special too. Pride and a strong need for recognition can get in its way.

Virgo (Aug 23–Sep 22). Earth, mutable, ruled by Mercury. Virgo is linked with attention to detail, usefulness, health and steady improvement. It tends to notice what needs fixing and to show care through practical help. Its challenge is worry and holding itself or others to impossible standards.

## Libra to Pisces

Libra (Sep 23–Oct 22). Air, cardinal, ruled by Venus. Libra is associated with fairness, beauty, partnership and diplomacy. It tends to weigh both sides and to look for harmony in any room. It can find decisions hard or avoid a conflict that needs to happen.

Scorpio (Oct 23–Nov 21). Water, fixed, ruled by Pluto in modern astrology and by Mars in traditional astrology. Scorpio is linked with intensity, depth, privacy and transformation. It tends to want the truth beneath the surface and to commit fully. Jealousy and difficulty letting go are its shadow side.

Sagittarius (Nov 22–Dec 21). Fire, mutable, ruled by Jupiter. Sagittarius is associated with adventure, travel, big questions and honesty. It often looks for meaning and the wider picture. It can be blunt, restless or quick to promise more than it can deliver.

Capricorn (Dec 22–Jan 19). Earth, cardinal, ruled by Saturn. Capricorn is linked with ambition, responsibility, structure and patience over the long haul. It tends to set goals and climb toward them step by step. It can become rigid or put work ahead of rest.

Aquarius (Jan 20–Feb 18). Air, fixed, ruled by Uranus in modern astrology and by Saturn in traditional astrology. Aquarius is associated with independence, originality, friendship and community. It often thinks about how things could work better for everyone. It can seem emotionally distant or hold tightly to its own ideas.

Pisces (Feb 19–Mar 20). Water, mutable, ruled by Neptune in modern astrology and by Jupiter in traditional astrology. Pisces is linked with imagination, compassion, spirituality and art. It tends to absorb the moods around it and to feel for others easily. Blurry boundaries and a wish to escape hard realities are its challenges.

## A worked example

Notice the pattern in the list. The elements repeat in the order fire, earth, air, water, and the modalities repeat in the order cardinal, fixed, mutable. Because four elements and three modalities never line up the same way twice, every sign has its own combination. Leo is the only fixed fire sign; Virgo is the only mutable earth sign.

Now say you were born on 5 August. The Sun was in Leo, so your Sun sign is Leo: fire, fixed, ruled by the Sun. Many astrologers would read that as a core drive toward warm, steady self-expression. But the Sun is only one point in your chart. Your Moon might be in Pisces and your Mercury, the planet of thinking and speaking, in Virgo. That would add emotional sensitivity and a careful, detail-minded way of communicating. This is why a single sign rarely tells the whole story.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Open the Charts tab and choose Birth Chart. The Big Three section shows your Sun sign along with your Moon and Rising signs, which the next lesson explains. Then scroll to Planet Positions, which lists the sign each planet was in when you were born. Pick three planets, find their signs in this lesson, and note each one's element, modality and ruler. You may find that your chart leans toward one element or one modality, which the element and modality lessons explore.

title: Sun, Moon & Rising
description: Why astrologers read your Sun, Moon and Rising signs together, what each one describes, and why the Rising sign needs your birth time.
content:
## Why three signs, not one

Most people know their Sun sign, the sign the Sun was in on their birthday. But a birth chart, the map of the sky at the exact moment and place you were born, places every planet in a sign. Three of those placements get special attention because together they give a quick, rounded sketch of a person. Astrologers call them the Big Three: the Sun, the Moon and the Rising sign.

A simple way to hold them in mind: the Sun describes who you are at your core, the Moon describes what you need to feel secure, and the Rising sign describes how you meet the world. Each one moves at a very different speed, which is why two people with the same Sun sign can feel so different.

## The Sun: your core self

The Sun spends about a month in each sign, so everyone born within the same few weeks shares a Sun sign. In astrology the Sun is associated with identity, vitality and purpose: what energizes you, what you want to be recognized for, and the self you grow into over a lifetime.

Example: a Sun in Capricorn is often read as a core identity built around responsibility and long-term goals. A person with this placement may feel most like themselves when they are working toward something that lasts.

## The Moon: your inner world

The Moon moves quickly. It spends about two and a half days in each sign and travels through all twelve in roughly 27 days. The Moon is associated with emotions, instincts, comfort, habits and what makes you feel safe. Many astrologers describe it as the part of you that shows up when you are tired, stressed or at home with the people closest to you.

Example: a Moon in Cancer is often read as a need for closeness, familiar surroundings and emotional care. A Moon in Aquarius, by contrast, is often read as a need for space and independence, even in close relationships.

Because the Moon changes sign every couple of days, your birth date usually narrows it to one sign. If the Moon changed signs on your birthday, your birth time settles which one it was.

## The Rising sign: how you meet the world

Your Rising sign, also called the Ascendant, is the sign that was coming up over the eastern horizon at the moment you were born. As Earth turns once a day, all twelve signs take turns on that horizon. So the Rising sign changes roughly every two hours. The exact timing varies with where on Earth you were born, because some signs take longer to rise than others at different latitudes.

The Rising sign is associated with first impressions, personal style and your instinctive approach to new situations. It is often compared to a front door: the part of you other people meet first.

The Rising sign also anchors the houses. Houses are twelve sections of the chart, each linked to an area of life such as home, work or relationships. The Rising sign marks the start of the first house, and the other houses follow from it. AstroNumeric uses the Placidus house system by default, the most common method in modern Western astrology.

This is why your birth time matters so much. If you do not know it, AstroNumeric assumes 12:00 noon. Your Sun and usually your Moon are still reliable, but your Rising sign and houses become estimates, and the app flags them so you know. A birth certificate or a family record is often the best place to find an accurate time.

## Putting the three together

Here is a worked example. Imagine someone with a Taurus Sun, an Aquarius Moon and Leo Rising.

• Taurus Sun: a core self associated with steadiness, patience and enjoying the physical world.
• Aquarius Moon: an inner need for freedom, fresh ideas and room to be different.
• Leo Rising: a warm, confident first impression, perhaps with a flair for how they present themselves.

Read together, this person might come across as bold and expressive, feel most at ease when they have independence, and at heart value security and routine. Those three can pull in different directions, and that tension is part of what makes the reading useful. It points to things worth noticing, not to a fixed personality.

Sometimes two of the three share a sign. Someone with a Libra Sun and Libra Rising has a double emphasis on Libra themes such as harmony and partnership. When all three differ, the person often recognizes each one in different settings: work, home and first meetings.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Open the Charts tab and choose Birth Chart. Your Big Three sit at the top of the chart: Sun, Moon and Rising. If you entered your birth details without a time, the app notes that the Rising sign and houses are estimates based on noon. From there, look at Houses to see how your Rising sign sets the starting point for all twelve houses, and at Planet Positions to see the signs of your other planets.

title: Sign Compatibility
description: How astrologers compare two people's signs, why no pairing is doomed, and why a full synastry chart says more than Sun signs.
content:
## What compatibility means in astrology

In astrology, compatibility is about how two people's energies meet. It looks at where their styles tend to flow easily, where they tend to rub against each other, and what each person can learn from the other. It applies to any relationship: partners, friends, family members, coworkers.

One point matters more than any other. No pairing is doomed. Plenty of lasting, loving relationships exist between signs that pop-culture charts call a bad match, and plenty of easy-looking matches do not work out. Astrology can describe the dynamics between two people. It cannot decide whether a relationship succeeds. That depends on the choices, effort and care of the people in it.

## Sun signs: a starting point

The simplest comparison uses Sun signs, the sign the Sun was in on each person's birthday. Astrologers usually start with the element of each sign: fire, earth, air or water.

• Same element (for example, two water signs): often an easy sense of being understood, because both people share a basic temperament. The risk is too much of one thing, such as two fire signs both racing ahead.
• Fire with air: air is often said to feed fire. Air brings ideas and fire brings enthusiasm, so the pair can spark each other.
• Earth with water: water is often said to nourish earth. Earth offers stability and water offers emotional depth.
• Fire or air with earth or water: these mixes speak different languages. Fire's speed can unsettle earth's patience, and air's logic can feel cool to water's feelings. The friction is real, but each person often supplies what the other lacks.

Astrologers also look at how far apart the two signs sit around the zodiac wheel. The distance forms an aspect, a meaningful angle between two points. Signs four apart (120 degrees, a trine) share an element and tend to flow easily. Signs two apart (60 degrees, a sextile) have friendly elements. Signs three apart (90 degrees, a square) share a modality, meaning they act in the same way (both starting, both holding on, or both adapting), which can create tension and motivation. Signs six apart (180 degrees, an opposition) face each other across the wheel and often attract and balance each other.

## A worked example

Take an Aries Sun and a Libra Sun. They are opposite signs, and both are cardinal, the modality associated with starting things. Aries tends to be direct and quick to act; Libra tends to be diplomatic and to weigh every side. They may clash over pace and decision-making. They may also learn a lot from each other: Aries can show Libra how to choose, and Libra can show Aries how to include others.

Now take a Taurus Sun and a Leo Sun. They are square to each other, and both are fixed, the modality associated with persistence. Neither likes to back down, so arguments can stall. Yet both value loyalty, and once committed, both tend to stay.

Neither description is a verdict. Each is a set of themes the pair might recognize and talk about.

## Why a full synastry chart says more

Sun signs are one planet out of many. Two people with a "difficult" Sun pairing may have Moons that blend beautifully, and the reverse is also common. That is why astrologers use synastry: laying two birth charts over each other and looking at the aspects between one person's planets and the other's.

• The Moon shows emotional needs. A harmonious link between two Moons often feels like being at home with someone.
• Venus shows affection and what a person values. Links involving Venus often describe attraction and shared tastes.
• Mars shows drive and how a person handles conflict and desire.
• Mercury shows communication, which matters in every relationship.
• Saturn shows commitment and responsibility. Its links can feel stabilizing, or heavy at times.

Each aspect is measured with an orb, the margin by which it can miss the exact angle and still count. Tighter aspects are usually read as stronger.

Astrologers also use a composite chart. It blends the two birth charts into a single chart using the midpoints between each pair of planets, and it is read as describing the relationship itself, as if the partnership were a third person with its own character.

## Using compatibility well

Compatibility works best as a conversation starter rather than a test. Useful questions include: Where do we naturally agree? Where do we tend to misunderstand each other? What does each of us need that the other might not think of? Used this way, it can build understanding. Used to rule people in or out, it tends to miss what actually keeps a relationship going.

It is also worth asking before using someone else's birth details. Birth dates and times are personal information.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Open Compatibility, which you can reach from the Charts tab or from Explore → Relationships, and enter the other person's birth details to see how your signs compare. For a deeper look, open Charts → Advanced Charts and choose Synastry to see the aspects between your two charts, or Composite to see the chart of the relationship itself. As with any birth chart, an accurate birth time for both people gives the most reliable result.

title: Cardinal, Fixed & Mutable
description: The three modalities describe how each sign tends to act: starting, sustaining or adapting. Learn which signs belong to each and why it matters.
content:
## What a modality is

Every zodiac sign has an element and a modality. The element (fire, earth, air or water) describes a sign's basic temperament: what kind of energy it carries. The modality, also called the quality or mode, describes how that energy tends to move. There are three modalities: cardinal, fixed and mutable.

Each modality contains four signs, one from each element. So there is a cardinal fire sign, a cardinal earth sign, a cardinal air sign and a cardinal water sign, and the same for fixed and mutable. Twelve signs, three modalities, four elements, and every sign has its own combination.

The modalities come from the seasons. In the tropical zodiac, which AstroNumeric uses, each season contains three signs. The first sign of a season is cardinal, the middle one is fixed, and the last one is mutable. The season names below follow the Northern Hemisphere, where this system began. In the Southern Hemisphere the seasons are reversed, but the signs and their modalities stay the same.

## Cardinal signs: starting things

The cardinal signs are Aries (Mar 21–Apr 19), Cancer (Jun 21–Jul 22), Libra (Sep 23–Oct 22) and Capricorn (Dec 22–Jan 19). The Sun enters each one at an equinox or a solstice, the turning points that begin spring, summer, autumn and winter.

Cardinal energy is associated with initiative, leadership and getting things moving. Each element starts in its own way:

• Aries starts with action and courage.
• Cancer starts by caring for people and creating a home base.
• Libra starts by reaching out to others and building partnerships.
• Capricorn starts with a plan and a long-term goal.

Cardinal signs often shine at the beginning of a project. Their common challenge is follow-through: once the exciting start is over, their attention may move to the next new thing.

## Fixed signs: keeping things going

The fixed signs are Taurus (Apr 20–May 20), Leo (Jul 23–Aug 22), Scorpio (Oct 23–Nov 21) and Aquarius (Jan 20–Feb 18). They fall in the middle of each season, when the weather is settled and steady.

Fixed energy is associated with persistence, loyalty, focus and depth. These signs tend to stay the course once they have committed.

• Taurus sustains through patience and steady effort.
• Leo sustains through heart and creative pride.
• Scorpio sustains through emotional intensity and determination.
• Aquarius sustains through conviction and loyalty to ideas and friends.

Their strength is reliability. Their challenge is change: fixed signs can dig in and become stubborn, even when a new approach would help.

## Mutable signs: adapting

The mutable signs are Gemini (May 21–Jun 20), Virgo (Aug 23–Sep 22), Sagittarius (Nov 22–Dec 21) and Pisces (Feb 19–Mar 20). They come at the end of each season, as one season gives way to the next.

Mutable energy is associated with flexibility, learning and adjustment. These signs tend to see many options and to adapt as situations change.

• Gemini adapts through ideas, questions and conversation.
• Virgo adapts by refining and improving what already exists.
• Sagittarius adapts by exploring new places and beliefs.
• Pisces adapts by sensing the mood and flowing with it.

Their strength is versatility. Their challenge is focus: mutable signs can scatter their energy, change direction too often, or struggle to decide.

## Modalities in your birth chart

Your birth chart, the map of the sky when you were born, places each planet in a sign, so you can count how many fall in each modality. Here is a worked example. Suppose a chart has these placements:

• Sun in Aries, Moon in Capricorn, Mercury in Pisces, Venus in Taurus, Mars in Cancer, Rising in Libra.

Aries, Capricorn, Cancer and Libra are cardinal, Taurus is fixed, and Pisces is mutable. That is four of six key placements in cardinal signs. Many astrologers would read this as someone who is often energized by new starts and comfortable taking the lead, who may need to work harder at finishing things and staying put. With only one fixed placement, patience and follow-through may be qualities this person consciously builds.

A chart that leans fixed is often read as steady and determined but slow to change. A chart that leans mutable is often read as adaptable and curious but sometimes unsettled. A balanced chart tends to draw on all three. Astrologers differ on how to weigh placements, so treat any count as a rough guide.

Modality also helps explain tension between planets. Two planets in signs of the same modality but different elements are usually square (90 degrees apart) or opposite (180 degrees apart). These aspects, or meaningful angles, are often read as friction that pushes for growth. For example, Aries and Cancer are both cardinal and square each other: two starters with very different styles.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Open the Charts tab, choose Birth Chart, and go to Planet Positions. Write down the sign of each planet from the Sun to Saturn, plus your Rising sign from the Big Three, and mark each one cardinal, fixed or mutable using the lists above. Then look at Key Aspects: squares and oppositions there often link signs of the same modality.

title: Fire Signs
description: Aries, Leo and Sagittarius: what fire stands for, how it shows up in a chart, and what a lot or little fire suggests.
content:
## What fire stands for

Astrology groups the twelve signs into four elements: fire, earth, air and water. Each element contains three signs and describes a basic temperament, a way of meeting life. Fire is the element of energy, enthusiasm and self-expression.

Think of a real flame. It gives warmth and light, it moves quickly, it needs fuel, and it can burn out if nothing feeds it. Astrologers associate fire signs with those same qualities: courage, spontaneity, optimism, confidence, and a strong urge to act on inspiration. Fire tends to lead with "let's try it" rather than "let's think about it."

## The three fire signs

The three fire signs share that spark but express it differently, because each has a different modality. The modality describes how a sign acts: cardinal signs start things, fixed signs sustain them, and mutable signs adapt them.

• Aries (Mar 21–Apr 19): cardinal fire, ruled by Mars. Aries is the spark that lights the fire. It is associated with initiative, bravery and directness. It likes to be first and tends to move before others have finished deciding.
• Leo (Jul 23–Aug 22): fixed fire, ruled by the Sun. Leo is the steady flame of a hearth. It is associated with warmth, generosity, creativity and loyalty. It tends to shine consistently and to want its efforts seen and appreciated.
• Sagittarius (Nov 22–Dec 21): mutable fire, ruled by Jupiter. Sagittarius is fire that spreads across open ground. It is associated with adventure, curiosity, big-picture thinking and honesty. It tends to chase meaning, new places and new ideas.

A ruling planet is the planet linked to a sign. Mars brings drive, the Sun brings vitality, and Jupiter brings growth and optimism, which helps explain each sign's flavor.

## Fire in a birth chart

Your Sun sign is only one part of the picture. Your birth chart, the map of the sky at the moment you were born, places every planet in a sign. So even if your Sun is in a water sign, you might have your Mars in Leo or your Rising sign in Aries. Each planet in a fire sign adds a touch of fire to that part of your life. Mercury in Sagittarius, for example, is often read as enthusiastic, big-picture thinking, and Venus in Aries as a direct, eager approach to affection.

Astrologers also look at element balance, meaning how many of your placements fall in each element.

One simple method many astrologers use is to give your Sun, your Moon and your Rising sign (the sign rising on the eastern horizon when you were born) two points each, and your Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn one point each. Uranus, Neptune and Pluto move so slowly that they stay in one sign for years, so everyone born around the same time shares them, and they are usually left out. Other astrologers count every planet equally or add the houses. There is no single agreed method, so treat any total as a rough guide.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a chart has the Sun in Leo (2 points), Moon in Taurus, Rising in Sagittarius (2 points), Mercury in Leo (1), Venus in Cancer, Mars in Aries (1), Jupiter in Gemini and Saturn in Capricorn. That gives fire 6 points out of a possible 11, which is a strong fire emphasis.

Some astrologers also note the fire houses. Houses are twelve sections of the chart, each linked to an area of life. The 1st, 5th and 9th houses share their themes with Aries, Leo and Sagittarius: the self, creativity and play, and travel and learning. Several planets in those houses can add a fiery tone even when the signs are not fire signs.

## A lot of fire, or very little

A chart with a lot of fire is often read as energetic, confident and warm. People with this emphasis tend to inspire others, bounce back quickly and throw themselves into new projects. The same heat has a cost: impatience, restlessness, speaking before thinking, and taking on so much that they burn out. Many astrologers suggest that fire-heavy people benefit from rest, routines that let them finish what they start, and friends who ask "are you sure?"

A chart with very little fire is often read as quieter in how it expresses drive. People with this pattern may find it harder to self-start, to put themselves forward or to trust a sudden impulse. They often prefer to plan, feel or think before acting, which can be a real strength. Many astrologers read a missing element as something a person either works to develop or seeks out in others, sometimes by being drawn to fiery friends or partners. Physical activity, creative play and small, low-risk chances to take the lead are common suggestions for bringing in more fire.

Neither pattern is better. A low-fire chart can still describe a bold person, especially if Mars, the planet of action, is strong in other ways. Element balance is one lens among many.

## Try it in AstroNumeric

Open the Charts tab and choose Birth Chart. Check the Big Three (your Sun, Moon and Rising signs) for any fire signs in your Sun, Moon or Rising, then go to Planet Positions and count how many planets fall in Aries, Leo or Sagittarius using the points method above. Look at Houses to see whether planets sit in your 1st, 5th or 9th house. If you want to track how your energy feels over time, Explore → Tools → Journal is a good place to note it.

title: Earth Signs
description: Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn: what earth stands for, how it shows up in a chart, and what a lot or little earth suggests.
content:
## What earth stands for

Astrology groups the twelve signs into four elements: fire, earth, air and water. Each element contains three signs and describes a basic temperament, a way of meeting life. Earth is the element of practicality, stability and the physical world.

Think of solid ground. It holds things up, it changes slowly, and with patience it grows food. Astrologers associate earth signs with those same qualities: reliability, patience, common sense, attention to the body and the senses, and a talent for turning ideas into something real. Earth tends to ask "how will this actually work?"

## The three earth signs

The three earth signs share that grounded quality but express it differently, because each has a different modality. The modality describes how a sign acts: cardinal signs start things, fixed signs sustain them, and mutable signs adapt them.

• Taurus (Apr 20–May 20): fixed earth, ruled by Venus. Taurus is the fertile field. It is associated with steadiness, comfort, pleasure in the senses, and building security over time. It tends to be loyal and calm, and slow to change its mind.
• Virgo (Aug 23–Sep 22): mutable earth, ruled by Mercury. Virgo is the careful gardener. It is associated with detail, skill, health, service and improvement. It tends to notice what needs attention and to fix it quietly.
• Capricorn (Dec 22–Jan 19): cardinal earth, ruled by Saturn. Capricorn is the mountain climber. It is associated with ambition, discipline, responsibility and long-term planning. It tends to set a goal and work toward it one step at a time.

A ruling planet is the planet linked to a sign. Venus brings enjoyment and value, Mercury brings analysis, and Saturn brings structure and patience, which helps explain each sign's flavor.

## Earth in a birth chart

Your Sun sign is only one part of the picture. Your birth chart, the map of the sky at the moment you were born, places every planet in a sign. So even if your Sun is in an air sign, you might have your Moon in Taurus or your Mars in Capricorn. Each planet in an earth sign adds a practical, steady quality to that part of your life. A Moon in Taurus, for example, is often read as finding comfort in routine and physical ease, and Mercury in Virgo as precise, methodical thinking.

Astrologers also look at element balance, meaning how many of your placements fall in each element.

One simple method many astrologers use is to give your Sun, your Moon and your Rising sign (the sign rising on the eastern horizon when you were born) two points each, and your Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn one point each. Uranus, Neptune and Pluto move so slowly that they stay in one sign for years, so everyone born around the same time shares them, and they are usually left out. Other astrologers count every planet equally or add the houses. There is no single agreed method, so treat any total as a rough guide.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a chart has the Sun in Gemini, Moon in Virgo (2 points), Rising in Capricorn (2 points), Mercury in Taurus (1), Venus in Taurus (1), Mars in Scorpio, Jupiter in Leo and Saturn in Capricorn (1). That gives earth 7 points out of a possible 11, a strong earth emphasis, even though the Sun sign is an air sign.

Some astrologers also note the earth houses. Houses are twelve sections of the chart, each linked to an area of life. The 2nd, 6th and 10th houses share their themes with Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn: money and possessions, daily work and health, and career and public life. Several planets in those houses can add an earthy tone even when the signs are not earth signs.

## A lot of earth, or very little

A chart with a lot of earth is often read as dependable, sensible and hardworking. People with this emphasis tend to be good with routines, money, their bodies and practical tasks, and others often rely on them. The same steadiness has a cost: they can get stuck, resist change, focus too much on security or possessions, or dismiss ideas that cannot be proved. Many astrologers suggest that earth-heavy people benefit from play, spontaneity and room to dream.

A chart with very little earth is often read as someone who lives more in ideas, feelings or inspiration than in practical detail. People with this pattern may find routines, budgets, schedules or looking after their physical health harder than others do. They may have plenty of ideas but struggle to follow through. Many astrologers read a missing element as something a person either works to develop or seeks out in others, sometimes by being drawn to steady, practical friends or partners. Simple structures, such as a regular sleep time, a written plan or a weekly check of finances, are common suggestions for bringing in more earth.

Neither pattern is better. A low-earth chart can still describe a very organized person, especially if Saturn, the planet of structure, is prominent. Element balance is one lens among many.

title: Air Signs
description: Gemini, Libra and Aquarius: what air stands for, how it shows up in a chart, and what a lot or little air suggests.
content:
## What air stands for

Astrology groups the twelve signs into four elements: fire, earth, air and water. Each element contains three signs and describes a basic temperament, a way of meeting life. Air is the element of thought, communication and connection.

Think of the air around you. You cannot see it, but it carries sound from one person to another, it moves constantly, and it fills every space. Astrologers associate air signs with those same qualities: curiosity, conversation, logic, fairness, social ease, and the ability to step back and see a situation from a distance. Air tends to ask "what do you think?" and "what if we tried it another way?"

## The three air signs

The three air signs share that mental, social quality but express it differently, because each has a different modality. The modality describes how a sign acts: cardinal signs start things, fixed signs sustain them, and mutable signs adapt them.

• Gemini (May 21–Jun 20): mutable air, ruled by Mercury. Gemini is the breeze that carries news. It is associated with curiosity, wit, learning and variety. It tends to gather information quickly and enjoy talking with all kinds of people.
• Libra (Sep 23–Oct 22): cardinal air, ruled by Venus. Libra is the balanced scale. It is associated with fairness, partnership, diplomacy and beauty. It tends to start conversations that bring people together and to look for a solution everyone can accept.
• Aquarius (Jan 20–Feb 18): fixed air, ruled by Uranus in modern astrology and by Saturn in traditional astrology. Aquarius is the steady wind of change. It is associated with independence, originality, friendship and ideals for a better society. It tends to hold firmly to its principles.

A ruling planet is the planet linked to a sign. Mercury brings communication, Venus brings harmony, and Uranus brings innovation (while Saturn, the traditional ruler, adds a sense of structure and principle), which helps explain each sign's flavor.

## Air in a birth chart

Your Sun sign is only one part of the picture. Your birth chart, the map of the sky at the moment you were born, places every planet in a sign. So even if your Sun is in an earth sign, you might have your Mercury in Gemini or your Rising sign in Libra. Each planet in an air sign adds a thoughtful, social quality to that part of your life. Venus in Libra, for example, is often read as valuing fairness and good company in relationships, and a Moon in Aquarius as needing space and room to think things through.

Astrologers also look at element balance, meaning how many of your placements fall in each element.

One simple method many astrologers use is to give your Sun, your Moon and your Rising sign (the sign rising on the eastern horizon when you were born) two points each, and your Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn one point each. Uranus, Neptune and Pluto move so slowly that they stay in one sign for years, so everyone born around the same time shares them, and they are usually left out. Other astrologers count every planet equally or add the houses. There is no single agreed method, so treat any total as a rough guide.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a chart has the Sun in Aquarius (2 points), Moon in Gemini (2 points), Rising in Cancer, Mercury in Aquarius (1), Venus in Pisces, Mars in Libra (1), Jupiter in Virgo and Saturn in Scorpio. That gives air 6 points out of a possible 11, a strong air emphasis.

Some astrologers also note the air houses. Houses are twelve sections of the chart, each linked to an area of life. The 3rd, 7th and 11th houses share their themes with Gemini, Libra and Aquarius: communication and learning, partnerships, and friends and communities. Several planets in those houses can add an airy tone even when the signs are not air signs.

## A lot of air, or very little

A chart with a lot of air is often read as bright, sociable and curious. People with this emphasis tend to be good talkers and listeners, quick learners and fair-minded mediators, and they often keep a calm head when others are upset. The same detachment has a cost: they can overthink, live in their heads, talk about feelings rather than feel them, or seem distant to people who want more emotional warmth. Many astrologers suggest that air-heavy people benefit from time in their bodies, such as walking or exercise, and from noticing emotions without analyzing them.

A chart with very little air is often read as more instinctive or hands-on than theoretical. People with this pattern may find it harder to step back from their feelings, to put their thoughts into words, or to see a situation from someone else's point of view. They often trust experience over debate, which can be a real strength. Many astrologers read a missing element as something a person either works to develop or seeks out in others, sometimes by being drawn to talkative, curious friends or partners. Reading, writing things down, and conversations with people who think differently are common suggestions for bringing in more air.

Neither pattern is better. A low-air chart can still describe a gifted communicator, especially if Mercury, the planet of thinking and speaking, is strong in other ways. Element balance is one lens among many.

title: Water Signs
description: Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces: what water stands for, how it shows up in a chart, and what a lot or little water suggests.
